title: Flowing everywhere
hook: the great Tao flows everywhere and claims nothing (Tao Te Ching 34)

segments.voice: Yesterday, knowing yourself: knowing others is discerning, knowing yourself is clear. Your line was know myself. When something flared up in you, did you ask what it was? Day one thousand ninety-six.

The last slide of a group presentation is the one with everybody's names on it. Sometimes there's one person on it who quietly fixed the spreadsheet at midnight, rewrote the clumsy paragraph, and sent the reminder that got everyone there on time. Their name is on the slide in the same size font as everyone else's. They didn't ask for more. Chapter thirty-four of the Tao Te Ching describes the Tao a lot like that person: everywhere in the work, and nowhere on the credits.
screen: `THE SLIDE WITH EVERYONE'S NAMES.` → `THE ONE WHO FIXED IT AT MIDNIGHT.` → `EVERYWHERE IN THE WORK, NOWHERE ON THE CREDITS.`

segments.voice: First, the flood. In James Legge's translation the chapter begins: "All-pervading is the Great Tao! It may be found on the left hand and on the right." The Chinese word behind all-pervading has the sense of water overflowing, spilling in every direction at once. Not a channel. A flood plain. Second, no claim. The chapter says all things depend on it to come into being, and it doesn't turn any of them away. And when the work is done, it doesn't claim the name of having done it. It clothes and feeds everything, and doesn't set itself up as their master. Third, small and great at once. Because it asks for nothing, the chapter says, it can be called small. And because everything returns to it without even knowing it's there, it can be called great. The same thing, named both ways. Fourth, the sage. The chapter ends by saying the wise person does great things in the same way: by never trying to make himself great. Not hiding. Not pretending to be nothing. Just not reaching for the name. Away from the book, credit is everywhere: at work, in families, online. A like, a thank-you, a name in the email. The chapter doesn't call wanting it wicked. It just describes something enormous that gives without keeping score, and suggests the wise do the same.
screen: `FOUND ON THE LEFT AND ON THE RIGHT.` · `WORK DONE, NO NAME CLAIMED.` · `CALLED SMALL, AND CALLED GREAT.` · `GREAT BY NOT MAKING ITSELF GREAT.` · then, large: `ALL-PERVADING IS THE GREAT TAO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give without claiming. Settle, and let your breath slow down. Bring to mind one small thing you could do for someone today that they may never trace back to you. Refill something that's running low. Fix a small thing that's been broken a while. Put in a good word when they're not around to hear it. Choose one. Then sit with the strange feeling of a gift with no name on it. Let it flow out, the way chapter thirty-four's Tao flows, left and right. The bell holds the time.
Flowing everywhere. Chapter thirty-four's great Tao, found on the left hand and the right, feeding everything and claiming none of it. Today's word.
Your line: claim nothing. Do one good thing today without your name on it, and don't mention it to anyone, even later. Day one thousand ninety-six.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter thirty-four as a model for giving without seeking credit: doing the work, letting it spread, and not claiming the name for it.

original.note: Chinese: overflowing, flooding; chapter thirty-four's word for the great Tao spreading left and right.

trapdoor: what you thought: flowing everywhere is a vague way of saying the Tao is everywhere.
what it means: the Tao spreads like a flood into everything, feeds it all, and claims none of it.
what a scholar hears: the chapter opens 大道氾兮, the great Tao overflowing, and plays small against great: the same Tao named both ways.

notes: Check the Legge 1891 quotation of chapter 34's opening word for word, including the exclamation mark.

Paraphrases of chapter 34: all things depend on it and none is refused; it does not claim the name of having done the work; it clothes all things and makes no assumption of being their lord; it may be named in the smallest and the greatest things; the sage accomplishes great things by not making himself great. Confirm each is fair.

Not claiming credit also appears in earlier chapters (2, 10, 17, among others) and may have been taught on earlier days; this day leads with the flood image and the small/great pairing to keep a fresh angle.
Original 氾 (fàn) rendered 'FAHN', glossed 'overflowing, flooding'. Some editions read 汎; confirm.
The group-presentation scene and the practice examples are the writer's illustrations.
